[1] The winter I was fourteen, Mr. Aurelio Pask's daughter telephoned my mother from Minneapolis and asked whether someone in our house could look in on her father each morning. He was eighty-one. He had lived alone at the end of Gorse Street since his wife died, and the daughter had been reading about falls. My mother said I would do it, and then she told me, which was the order in which most things in our house were decided that year. "Don't make it a visit," she said. "He'll hate a visit. Find a reason."

[2] I found a different reason every morning for a week. I came to borrow a snow shovel we did not need, then to return the shovel, then to ask whether he had seen our cat, which had not left the house since October. Mr. Pask answered the door each time in a cardigan buttoned to the throat, listened to my reason with his head tilted as if it were a radio station coming in faintly, and supplied whatever I had asked for. On the Friday he handed me the shovel again before I had opened my mouth.

[3] "You may as well keep it on the porch," he said. "Save us both the walk."

[4] That was as close as he came to saying he knew. He did not say it was kind of my mother, or that his daughter worried too much, or that he was perfectly all right, which were the three remarks I had prepared answers to. Instead, on the Saturday, he asked whether I could read a thermometer.

[5] Behind his house, nailed to the north side of the woodshed where the sun never reached it, hung a glass thermometer in a white wooden box with slatted sides. Every morning at seven since 1958, Mr. Pask had written down what it said, along with the wind, the sky, and the depth of snow on a stake he had driven into the garden. The notebooks filled a shelf in his kitchen: green clothbound ledgers, one per year, their spines lettered in white ink. He told me the town had once had an official weather observer, a pharmacist named Lindqvist, and that when Lindqvist retired nobody had been appointed in his place, so for a while there had been two records and now there was one.

[6] "Nobody asks for it," he said. "That isn't the point of it."

[7] He did not say what the point was, and I did not ask, because I was fourteen and the question seemed to me either too obvious or too rude. I learned the procedure instead. You did not touch the box. You read the mercury at eye level, so the line did not jump when you moved your head. You wrote the figure before you wrote anything else, because the figure was the only thing you could not go back and check. Sky and wind could be argued about afterward; the thermometer would have moved on.

[8] For the rest of December I arrived at ten to seven, and he came out in his boots and stood beside me while I read. Some mornings he wrote what I called out; some mornings he wrote nothing until he had leaned in and read it himself. I minded this at first, and then I noticed he did the same thing with his own readings, leaning close, straightening, leaning again, as though the number had to be caught twice to count.

[9] In January he caught the flu that was going around the school, and his daughter flew in and stayed nine days. On the first of those mornings I stood at the side gate, unsure whether I was still wanted, and she came out in her father's cardigan and said he had asked whether "the boy" had done the reading yet. I did it alone. I wrote the figure first. Then I wrote the wind, the sky, and the snow depth, in a hand I made as square and small as his, and when I came to the column at the right edge of the page, the one he called Remarks, I left it empty, because I did not think it was mine to fill.

[10] When he was well again, he went through those nine days with a pencil. He changed nothing. Beside the last of them, in the Remarks column, he wrote a single word, which I did not see until March, when he sent me home with that year's ledger so I could "see how a winter looks laid end to end." The word was "Relieved." I have never decided whether he meant himself.

correct_answer: was making out something behind the narrator's stated reason that went unsaid.

[1] Every election requires a small, mostly unnoticed decision that has nothing to do with any candidate's record: someone has to decide whose name goes first. For a long time, many American jurisdictions settled the matter by the simplest rule available. Incumbents went first in some places, the governor's party in others, and in many the alphabet decided. Those rules looked neutral, and in one sense they were, since they were written before anyone knew who would be running. Whether they were neutral in effect is a question political scientists have spent several decades trying to answer.

[2] The suspicion is old. Researchers who study surveys had long known that when people are asked to choose from a list, the position of an option can affect how often it is chosen, especially when the person choosing has little reason to prefer one option over another. A voter facing a ballot is, in many races, exactly that person. Few voters arrive at the polls with views about the county coroner or the third seat on the water board. If position nudges anyone, it should nudge them.

[3] Proving it is harder than suspecting it. The trouble with the alphabet is that it does not vary. If every ballot in a state lists Adams above Zimmerman, and Adams wins, there is no way to know what would have happened had Zimmerman been listed first; any comparison between candidates is a comparison between different people with different campaigns. Early studies that pooled results from many races and noticed that first-listed candidates won slightly more often were open to exactly this objection. Perhaps the first-listed candidates were, by some accident, the stronger candidates.

[4] What made the question answerable was a reform designed to answer a complaint about fairness, not a research problem. Some states began rotating the order of names, so that a candidate who appears first in one precinct or district appears lower in another. California went further: before each election its secretary of state draws a randomized alphabet that sets the order of names, and for statewide offices that order is then rotated across the state's assembly districts. Rotation of this kind does what no one could do with a fixed alphabet. It shows the same candidates, in the same race, on the same day, to comparable voters in different positions. Any difference in how they fare by position can no longer be blamed on who the candidates are.

[5] Studies built on rotation have produced a fairly consistent picture, though not the dramatic one the old suspicion implied. In general elections for prominent offices, where most voters know the candidates and many follow a party label, the advantage of being listed first tends to be small, often too small to detect. The effect grows where voters have less to go on: in primaries, where every candidate shares a party; in nonpartisan contests for local offices; and among minor candidates whom few voters have heard of. In those races, researchers have repeatedly found first-listed candidates gaining a measurable share of the vote, commonly estimated at a few percentage points or less. That is not much in a landslide, but it is larger than the winning margin in a meaningful number of close contests.

[6] The findings did not settle the policy argument so much as change its shape. Before rotation, defenders of fixed orders could reasonably say that no one had shown the order mattered. Afterward, the argument shifted to whether an effect of that size is a problem worth the cost of solving. Rotation is not free: it means printing many versions of each ballot, and it complicates the work of checking that every version is correct. Some officials have argued that a few points in low-profile races is a fair price for a simple system. Courts in several states, asked to rule on fixed orders that regularly favored one party's candidates, have disagreed with one another about whether such an advantage amounts to a legal harm.

[7] Underneath the numbers sits a point that is easy to miss. The ballot-order effect is largest exactly where voters know least, which means it is less a measure of how ballots are designed than of how much information voters bring to them. A perfectly rotated ballot removes the unfairness between candidates, since no one gains from position on average, but it does not remove the guessing. It distributes the guessing evenly. Whether that counts as a solution depends on what one thought the problem was.

[1] For most of its history, dance has been kept the way gossip is kept: by passing it on. A dancer learns a role from someone who danced it, who learned it from someone who danced it before, and the work survives as long as the chain of bodies does. When the chain breaks, the dance does not go into storage. It goes. We have the names of hundreds of ballets from the eighteenth century and can perform almost none of them as they were seen.

[2] I reconstruct dances for a living, which means I spend most of my working life on the far side of a broken chain. My current project is a nine-minute solo called Threshold, made in 1934 by a choreographer named Hilde Varga and last performed, as far as anyone can establish, in 1951. No film of it exists. No one who saw it is alive to describe it. What exists is a score: forty-one pages of notation, written by Varga's assistant in a system published in the late 1920s that records movement as symbols on a vertical staff, one column for each part of the body, read from the bottom of the page upward.

[3] People who learn that a dance can be written down tend to assume the hard part is over. It is not. A notation score is something like a musical score in that it tells you a great deal and leaves a great deal more to the performer, but the proportions are different. A pianist reading Bach is helped by three centuries of people playing Bach; there is a living sense of how fast "fast" is, how loud a passage marked loud should be. I have no such inheritance for Varga. The score tells me that the right arm rises forward to shoulder height over two counts. It does not tell me whether the arm is reaching for something or pushing something away, and those are two different dances.

[4] So reconstruction is detective work in the gaps. I read Varga's letters, in which she complains about dancers who "decorate." I study photographs of her company, posed in a studio, each dancer frozen at the top of a gesture, so that the photograph shows the shape and nothing about how the dancer arrived at it. I look at the dances her students made after she stopped working, on the theory that habits outlast intentions. And then I make choices, and I write them down beside the score, so that the next person can see where Varga ends and I begin.

[5] That last practice is the one I would defend most strongly, and the one most often skipped. A reconstruction that hides its guesses presents itself as the original recovered, and audiences, reasonably, believe it. Within a generation the guesses have hardened into tradition. The next reconstructor, finding a performance in living memory, learns from that instead of from the score, and the chain that seemed to have been repaired turns out to have been replaced.

[6] There is an opposite risk, and some of my colleagues fall into it. They treat the score as a set of legal instructions and perform only what is written, filling the gaps with nothing: arms that rise exactly to shoulder height on exactly two counts, faces held blank because the notation records no expression. The result is accurate in the way a transcript of a conversation is accurate, and it bears the same relation to the conversation. Varga, who complained so bitterly about decoration, would not have complained about this. She would simply not have recognized it.

[7] I have come to think the score is best understood not as the dance but as testimony about it: the account of a careful witness who was in the room, who saw everything and was able to record only some of it. You do not ignore such a witness, and you do not take its silences as evidence that nothing happened. You question it, and you say plainly which parts of your account come from the witness and which come from you.

[8] In April the dancer I am working with will perform Threshold for the first time in more than seventy years. The program note will say that it is a reconstruction. It will not be able to say how much of what the audience sees Varga would have recognized, because no one can say that. What it can do is point to the annotated score, where every choice I made is marked in red, and where anyone who disagrees with me can begin again.

[1] For most of its existence a surge-type glacier behaves like any other, creeping downhill at anywhere from a few centimetres to perhaps a metre a day. Then, after a quiet interval that can last a decade or several, it abruptly speeds up by a factor of ten or more, pushing its front forward within a season or two, before it slows again and begins another long quiet phase. Only around one glacier in a hundred behaves this way, and surge-type glaciers are crowded into a few regions, among them Alaska and the Yukon, Svalbard, Iceland, and the Karakoram.

[2] The best-watched surge so far is still the one at Variegated Glacier in Alaska in 1982 and 1983, which a research team had been monitoring for years in anticipation. What the team found pointed to water at the bed. During the surge, water pressure measured in boreholes stayed close to the pressure exerted by the weight of the ice itself, high enough to lift the glacier partly off its bed. Dye poured into the glacier took far longer to emerge at the front than it did in normal flow, which meant the water was travelling slowly through a widespread network of cavities rather than quickly through a few large tunnels.

[3] That difference is the heart of the explanation. In ordinary flow, meltwater carves efficient channels under the ice that drain it away and keep pressure low. If those channels close, as they may in winter when little meltwater arrives to hold them open, water backs up into a broad, poorly connected system of gaps; pressure rises, friction at the bed falls, and the ice slides. The faster it slides, the more it opens new gaps and squeezes channels shut, so the change feeds itself.

[4] The end of the Variegated surge was as sudden as its start. In early summer of 1983, floods of muddy water burst from the front of the glacier and the ice slowed sharply within days, as if a plug had been pulled. On this account, the efficient channels had re-formed, the stored water escaped through them, and the ice settled back onto its bed.

Passage B

[1] The water story fits Alaska well. It fits Svalbard poorly, and Svalbard holds a large share of the world's surge-type glaciers. Surges there build up over years rather than months, can take several years to run their course, and reach peak speeds far lower than those recorded at Variegated. They do not end in a single burst. A switch that flips on and off within a season seems an unlikely explanation for an event that unfolds over the better part of a decade.

[2] A growing number of glaciologists think the deeper control is heat. Whether a glacier can slide at all depends on whether its bed is frozen to the rock beneath or sits at the melting point. Much of a cold-region glacier's bed is frozen fast; there, meltwater cannot lubricate the bed, because none reaches it. But ice is a good insulator, and as a glacier thickens during its quiet phase, heat from the Earth's interior and from the friction of slow flow accumulates at the bed. Eventually a patch of the bed reaches the melting point. Water produced there lowers the friction, faster flow produces more frictional heat, more of the bed thaws, and the surge spreads.

[3] Recent work has tried to fold both pictures into a single accounting of heat and water at the bed, in which a glacier surges when it gains them faster than it can get rid of them and slows when the balance tips back. In that accounting, surge-type glaciers cluster where they do because those climates fall within a band: cold enough that beds are not kept thawed and well drained, but not so cold and dry that the heat never builds. The water switch does not disappear. It becomes one way a glacier can lose its balance, quickly in mild, wet Alaska and slowly in cold, dry Svalbard.

[4] That revision changes what a surge-type glacier is. Rather than a special kind of glacier, it becomes an ordinary glacier in a particular climate, and if the climate shifts, glaciers that have never surged may begin to, while others stop.
prompt: How does the combined account in Passage B, paragraph 3, treat the mechanism described in Passage A?
choices: It rejects the mechanism, holding that water at the bed plays no part in starting a surge.
It accepts the mechanism for Svalbard but substitutes a heat-based one for Alaska.
It keeps the mechanism as one route to a surge within a wider balance of heat and water.
It treats the mechanism as the deeper cause, of which built-up heat is only one symptom.
correct_answer: It keeps the mechanism as one route to a surge within a wider balance of heat and water.
explanation: Passage B says "The water switch does not disappear. It becomes one way a glacier can lose its balance," inside "a single accounting of heat and water at the bed." It does not reject the role of water. It reverses neither the regions - the switch is fast "in mild, wet Alaska," which is where A's account fits - nor the hierarchy: heat is called "the deeper control," so the water switch is not the deeper cause.
